s: Coronis, Phlegyas’s Thessalian daughter, is loved by Apollo but chooses Ischys against her father’s judgment; Apollo kills her, then rescues their child Aesculapius from her burning pyre.
Thessaly was the name Antiphus son of Thessalus gave to the country he took possession of among the Pelasgians.

Caeneus, formerly a woman, became an invulnerable man after intercourse with Poseidon. In battle with centaurs, he killed many and ignored wounds until the survivors surrounded him and buried him in the earth with fir trees.

Athena is a goddess, born from Zeus’s head after he swallowed the pregnant Metis. Raised by Triton, she learned the arts of war with Pallas. After wounding Pallas in a quarrel, she made a wooden image in Pallas’s likeness, put the aegis around it, and honored it beside Zeus; the image is identified as her Palladium. She also flayed the giant Pallas for a shield and received the Gorgon’s head from Perseus. In the contest with Poseidon for Attica, she planted the olive-tree, called Cecrops as witness, and won Attica by the verdict of the twelve gods; she then named Athens after herself. Seeking weapons from Hephaestus, she was pursued by him; Erichthonius was produced from what fell to the ground. One account calls her his mother. She raised him secretly, hid him in a chest entrusted to Pandrosus, and later raised him in her precinct; he established her wooden image on the acropolis. Before Alexander, she competed in a judgment and offered victory in war. Her anger at Ajax’s impiety brought destruction on Greek ships through a storm and thunderbolt. At Ilium, Locrian maidens were sent as suppliants to propitiate her. She also gave Hercules a robe and fought Odysseus before Apollo reconciled them.

Chiron is a centaur, offspring of Cronus and Philyra, and a healer who teaches Aesculapius. He advises and repeatedly aids Peleus, helping him seize Thetis, saving him, restoring his sword, and giving an ash spear, then raises Achilles. He also restores Phoenix’s sight, unfolding as a protector, teacher, and healer.
Theseus’s son by an Amazon and Phaedra’s stepson rejects Phaedra’s advances, is falsely accused of assault, and dies when Poseidon’s bull frightens his horses.
Glaucus, son of Minos and Hippolochus, Lycian leader and Trojan ally, is resurrected by Polyidus and exchanges arms with Diomedes.

Minos is a king and ruler of Crete, husband of Pasiphae, father of Phaedra and Androgeus, and owner of Naucrate. He becomes king, passes laws, receives Talos from Hephaestus, and possesses a swift dog. After failing to sacrifice a bull to Poseidon, he shuts the Minotaur in the Labyrinth. Pasiphae bewitches him because he cohabited with many women; when he seeks Procris, her Circaean root prevents the harm to women who sleep with him, and he gives her the dog and a straight-flying dart. Androgeus’s death leads Minos to attack Athens, capture Megara, kill Megareus, drown Scylla, and demand seven youths and seven maidens as food for the Minotaur. He receives Daedalus, but after Theseus and his company escape, imprisons Daedalus and Icarus. Pursuing Daedalus with a spiral shell, he finds him with Cocalus and is killed by the daughters of Cocalus with boiling pitch.

The Cyclopes are a people inhabiting their land who forge thunderbolts for Zeus. After they make Zeus’s thunderbolt, Apollo slays them when Zeus uses it against Aesculapius; later those near Polyphemus’s cave leave after misunderstanding his cry.
Admetus, son of Pheres, is a man served by Apollo at Pherae for a year; Apollo tended his herds and made every female cattle bear twins.
is_fashioned_by Cyclopes [for Zeus] The thunderbolt was made by the Cyclopes for Zeus. Zeus used it to strike Aesculapius.

is_practiced_by Aesculapius [at a highly developed level] Aesculapius learned the healing art from Chiron and practiced it extensively. Zeus feared that people might acquire the healing art from Aesculapius and use it to rescue one another.

l: resurrection of the dead, The Library
s: Aesculapius raised some dead people by using blood from the Gorgon’s veins that he had received from Athena. The text names Capaneus, Lycurgus, Hippolytus, Tyndareus, Hymenaeus, and Glaucus as people reported to have been raised by him.
Apollo killed Coronis after she chose to live with Ischys. As Coronis was burning, Apollo rescued her child from the pyre.

l: Apollo’s slaying of the Cyclopes, The Library
s: Apollo slew the Cyclopes because Zeus had struck Aesculapius with a thunderbolt. Zeus then intended to hurl Apollo into Tartarus, but ordered him instead to serve Admetus for a year.

l: Apollo’s servitude to Admetus, The Library
s: An appendix entry recounts Apollo serving Admetus at Pherae for a year by Zeus’s command, tending herds and causing female cattle to bear twins.
Aeolus, king of Aeolia and Zeus-appointed keeper of winds, entertains Odysseus, gives him a wind-filled ox-hide bag, then drives him away when gods oppose his return.
is_a Naiad nymph Batia was the daughter of Teucer. She married Dardanus.

Hippocoon was a son of Oebalus and the nymph Batia, according to one genealogy. With the help of his sons, he expelled Tyndareus and Icarius from Lacedaemon. Heracles later killed Hippocoon and his sons.
Alexander abducts Helen from Sparta. Sparta was ruled by Menelaus after Tyndareus gave him the kingdom. Alexander visited Sparta and persuaded Helen to leave with him.

Hercules, also named Alcides and called a hero, is a figure defined by exceptional combat, service, travel, and eventual immortality. As an infant, Hera sends serpents to kill him; later she drives him mad, and his madness leads him to burn the children he had by Megara. He is married to Megara, gives her to Iolaus, and later marries Hebe. He has a twin, Iphicles, and is recorded as father of several children by Megara, Epicaste, Chalciope, Astyoche, Thespius’s daughters, and others. As punishment for murdering his children, he serves Eurystheus for twelve years. His labours are described as ten, completed in eight years and a month, though another record calls them twelve. They include killing the Nemean lion and Lernaean hydra, using the hydra’s gall on his arrows, bringing the Cerynitian hind and Erymanthian boar to Mycenae, cleansing the cattle-yard of Augeas, shooting the Stymphalian birds, bringing the Cretan bull, the mares of Diomedes, Hippolyte’s belt, and Cerberus, and killing Geryon or driving away Geryon’s kine. He receives aid or equipment from Athena, the Sun, and Zeus, including brazen castanets and a golden goblet for crossing the ocean. Beyond these services, he kills many enemies and monsters, battles centaurs, fights the Amazons at Themiscyra, sides with the gods against the giants, captures Ilium and Oechalia, conquers Thasos, restores Tyndareus, founds Abdera and the Olympian games, rescues Theseus from Hades, and resurrects Alcestis. He is initiated in the Mysteries of Eleusis and serves Omphale as a slave. His later story includes a poisoned robe, torture, burning himself on Mount Oeta, and obtaining immortality; he is eventually reconciled to Hera.

Leda was the daughter of Thestius and the wife of Tyndareus. Zeus approached her in the form of a swan, and Tyndareus also cohabited with her on the same night. She bore Pollux and Helen to Zeus, and Castor and Clytaemnestra to Tyndareus.

Penelope is the daughter of Icarius and Periboea, wife of Odysseus or Ulysses, and mother of Telemachus; she is also said to bear Poliporthes or Polypoethes to Ulysses. When suitors, including men from Ithaca, believe Ulysses dead, they pressure her to remarry. She delays them for three years by weaving Laertes’ shroud by day and undoing it by night. Ulysses returns, kills the suitors, reveals himself, and is recognized by her. Later traditions diverge: Telegonus takes her and Odysseus’s corpse to Circe and marries her, after which Circe sends them to the Islands of the Blest; other accounts allege seduction, exile to Icarius, or her death.

Ulysses is a Greek commander, leader of the Cephallenians, son of Laertes and Anticlea, husband of Penelope, and father of Poliporthes, Telegonus, and Leontophonus. He first secures his marriage to Penelope by promising to help Tyndareus, then tries to evade the expedition against Troy by feigning madness. Exposed after Telemachus is threatened, he joins the Greeks and repeatedly acts through strategy, deception, and persuasion: he finds Achilles by a trumpet blast, engineers Palamedes’ ruin, helps obtain Philoctetes and his bow, captures Helenus, steals the Palladium with Diomedes, wins Achilles’ arms, and invents, enters, and leads the men in the Wooden Horse. After Troy’s fall he receives Hecuba. His return is marked by raids, encounters with the Lotus-eaters, Laestrygones, Polyphemus, Circe, the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, and Calypso. He calls himself Nobody against Polyphemus, uses Moly against Circe’s enchantments, and is bound to the mast to hear the Sirens safely. At last he returns to Ithaca disguised as a beggar and, aided by Telemachus and Eumaeus, kills Penelope’s suitors. Following Tiresias’s directions, he travels and sacrifices to propitiate Poseidon. In the final account, Telegonus unknowingly wounds him with a sting-ray-spined spear while defending cattle in Ithaca, and Ulysses dies from the wound; other records give an exile to Aetolia as an alternative ending.

Clytaemnestra, daughter of Tyndareus and Leda, becomes Agamemnon’s wife after he kills her former husband Tantalus and their child. Asked to send Iphigenia to Aulis under a false marriage pretext, she does so. She later gives Agamemnon a sleeveless, neckless shirt, helps kill him and Cassandra, and is eventually killed by Orestes.

Agamemnon is a king of the Mycenaeans and leader of the Greeks against Troy. Rescued with Menelaus by their nurse and taken to Sicyon, he is later helped by Menelaus to expel Thyestes. He becomes Tyndareus’s son-in-law by marrying Clytaemnestra, after killing her former husband Tantalus and their newborn child. Listed among Helen’s suitors, he later answers Menelaus’s request for war by reminding the suitors’ kings of their oaths, raising Greek levies, commanding the whole army, and bringing one hundred ships. During the expedition he reads a forged letter, finds gold, and hands Palamedes to the allies to be stoned; he is also called an accomplice in Palamedes’s killing. Having angered Artemis through his claim about shooting a deer and Atreus’s unsacrificed golden lamb, he deceitfully sends for his daughter Iphigenia, saying she is promised to Achilles. After Troy’s sack, he receives Cassandra, quarrels with Menelaus, returns with Cassandra to Mycenae, and is murdered by Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra; Cassandra is killed too.

A goddess associated with a Taurian wooden image, Artemis angered by Agamemnon demanded his fairest daughter’s sacrifice, then took Iphigenia to the Taurians as priestess, replacing her with a deer; she caused Adonis’s death.

Pollux, son of Leda and said also to have been born to Zeus and Leda, was a boxer and one of the Dioscuri with Castor. With Castor he recovered Helen, married a daughter of Leucippus, and had Mnesileus by Phoebe. He killed Lynceus with a spear, was carried to heaven by Zeus, and refused immortality while Castor was dead.

Helen is a daughter of Zeus, variously by Leda or Nemesis, and in the Nemesis tradition is born from an egg. As a twelve-year-old, she is abducted by Theseus, with Pirithous, and taken from Sparta to Aphidnae or Athens; Pollux and Castor later recover her. She becomes the object of many Greek heroes’ suit, and Tyndareus chooses Menelaus as her bridegroom. She marries Menelaus and has Hermione and, according to some, Nicostratus. After Menelaus departs for Crete, Alexander persuades Helen to leave Sparta or carries her off. Her removal prompts the Greek expedition: the Greeks prepare to campaign in the second year after her rape, and their embassy demands her restoration, which the Trojans refuse. In an alternative account, Hermes takes the real Helen to Egypt at Zeus’s will, while Alexander brings a cloud-made phantom to Troy. During the war, Helen recognizes Odysseus when he enters the Trojan city disguised as a beggar and helps him steal the Palladium. She also walks around the Wooden Horse, calling to the Greek leaders in imitations of their wives’ voices. Afterward Menelaus kills Deiphobus, takes Helen to the ships, and, in accounts locating her with Proteus in Egypt, finds her there and returns with her to Sparta. Finally, Hera makes Menelaus immortal, and Helen goes with him to the Elysian Fields.

Castor, a son of Leda, was said to have been born to Tyndareus and Leda. A warrior, he and his brother Pollux were called the Dioscuri, recovered Helen from Aphidnae, and took cattle and booty to Messene. He married a daughter of Leucippus and had Anogon by Hilaira. Found hiding by Lynceus, he was killed by Idas, and is alternately among gods and mortals.

Theseus is a son of Aegeus and Aethra, born in Troezen. Raised with Aegeus’s sword and sandals as tokens of his parentage, he comes of age by moving a stone to recover them and travels on foot to Athens. On that journey he clears the road and the Isthmus of Corinth of evildoers, killing Periphetes, Sinis, Sciron, Phaea, and others; after killing Periphetes, he takes and carries his iron club. His sword identifies him to Aegeus. As part of the Cretan tribute, Theseus enters the Labyrinth, uses Ariadne’s clue of thread to escape, and kills the Minotaur with his fists. Following Aegeus’s death, he takes Athenian sovereignty as king, kills the fifty sons of Pallas and other opponents of his rule, and is also credited with killing Cercyon, Damastes, and the Marathonian bull. He plots against Medea, is tried at Delphinium in a different tradition, and is exiled to Troezen for a year with Phaedra. His later life is marked by warfare, marriages, children, and risky alliances. He joins Hercules against the Amazons, carries off Antiope or Melanippe, defeats Amazons with the Athenians, and has Hippolytus by an Amazon. He marries Phaedra and fathers Acamas and Demophon; believing Phaedra’s accusation against Hippolytus, he prays to Poseidon for Hippolytus’s death. With Pirithous, he fights and kills many centaurs at Pirithous’s wedding. The pair make a pact to marry daughters of Zeus, abduct Helen, and descend into Hades seeking Persephone for Pirithous. There Theseus is deceived and bound by serpents to the Chair of Forgetfulness, until Heracles brings him back. While he is in Hades, Castor and Pollux recover Helen from Aphidnae and take Aethra captive. He is further said to receive Oedipus and capture Thebes with the Athenians. Menestheus eventually drives him from Athens. The records end by saying Lycomedes kills Theseus, although one record instead says Theseus kills Lycomedes.

Aethra lay with Aegeus and Poseidon after Aegeus was made drunk. Aegeus instructed her to rear a child without saying whose he was, send him with sword, sandals when he moved a rock. She had Theseus; captive of Thracians.

Helen’s suitors were Greek kings and heroes who came to Sparta seeking her hand. Because Tyndareus feared their rivalry, he made them swear to defend whichever bridegroom was chosen against wrong concerning the marriage.

Diomedes, son of Tydeus, is a Greek leader who fights at Troy. During the war he wounds Aphrodite while she helps Aeneas, exchanges arms with Glaucus, and with Ulysses kills Dolon and Rhesus. He accompanies Odysseus to Lemnos, enters Troy, and brings the Palladium to the ships. After Troy’s destruction, he sails with Nestor and Menelaus and has a prosperous voyage.
has_a_prosperous_voyage Greek ships [in company with Diomedes] Nestor sailed with Diomedes and Menelaus. He and Diomedes had a prosperous voyage.
Amphilochus, son of Alcmaeon, leaves his ship in Ilium, travels to Colophon, is storm-driven to Mopsus, and dies with him fighting for a kingdom.
held sovereignty of Athens [given to him by the Dioscuri] The Dioscuri brought Menestheus back and gave him the sovereignty of Athens. Menestheus later drove Theseus from Athens.

l: Ajax son of Oileus, The Library
s: violates Cassandra [while she clings to the wooden image of Athena] Ajax the Locrian violated Cassandra while she clung to the wooden image of Athena.
Ares, a deity and father in several genealogies, kills Halirrhothius, is tried and acquitted before twelve gods, opposes Odysseus, and is bound by Otus and Ephialtes.

Pirithous, son of Ixion, marries Hippodamia and fights drunken centaurs with Theseus after they attack her at their wedding. Allied with Theseus in seeking daughters of Zeus, he helps abduct Helen, descends into Hades to seek Persephone, and is bound there forever by serpents.
Podalirius travels by land from Ilium to Colophon, consults Delphi about settling, and settles safely in the mountain-surrounded Carian Chersonese.

Philoctetes, son of Poeas, leads Olizonians against Troy and possesses the bow of Heracles. Bitten by a water-snake during a sacrifice to Apollo at Tenedos, he is abandoned by the Greeks on Lemnos because of his incurable, foul-smelling wound. He survives by shooting birds with the bow. During the ten-year war, Odysseus persuades him to sail to Troy after obtaining the bow and arrows by craft; Podalirius heals him, and he kills Alexander with them. After later wanderings, he reaches Italy, fights near Croton and Thurium, settles at Crimissa, founds a sanctuary of Apollo Alaios, and dedicates his bow there.

Eurypylus denotes several figures: son of Evaemon, who sought Helen, led the Ormenians against Troy, and was wounded; son of Hercules by Eubote; son of Poseidon, king of Cos, slain by Hercules; son of Telephus, who commanded Mysians for the Trojans and was slain by Neoptolemus; and son of Temenus, who hired murderers against his father.
Protesilaus first lands from his ship, kills many barbarians, is killed by Hector, then returns from Hades through Hermes and resurrects the dead.

Iphiclus, son of Phylacus and father of Podarces, in one version detained kine and imprisoned Melampus for a year before releasing him. Fright from Phylacus's knife caused childlessness; ten days of rusted-knife wine restored virility.

Menelaus is Helen’s husband and king of Sparta, chosen by Tyndareus among her suitors. He marries Helen, has Hermione and, in some accounts, Nicostratus, and reigns in Sparta after Tyndareus cedes the kingdom. Earlier, he is rescued with Agamemnon and taken to Sicyon; he also travels to Crete for Catreus’s funeral rites. After Helen’s abduction, his central purpose is her restoration: he asks Agamemnon to raise a Greek expedition, helps recruit allies, leads the Lacedaemonians with sixty ships, and goes with Ulysses to Troy to demand Helen and the property. Though the envoys are threatened, Antenor saves them. Menelaus fights Alexander in single combat and is wounded by Pandarus, breaking the truce. He leads Greeks against Troy, recognizes and rescues Glaucus with Ulysses, kills Deiphobus, and leads Helen from Troy to the ships. On the return, he urges departure rather than sacrifice to Athena, but storms scatter his fleet. Left with five ships, he reaches Egypt and wanders through Libya, Phoenicia, Cyprus, Crete, and Egypt. After eight years he returns through Mycenae to Sparta and regains his kingdom. One account says he discovers the real Helen in Egypt; the records also say he rescues Helen from Troy. He ultimately reigns in Sparta with Helen and goes with her to the Elysian Fields.

Atreus, spouse of Aerope, keeps a golden lamb despite vowing it to Artemis. After Zeus reverses the sun, he gains Mycenae and banishes Thyestes, then murders and serves Thyestes’ sons to him. Aegisthus kills Atreus and restores the kingdom to Thyestes.

Ajax was a Greek hero, son of Telamon and Periboea, named after an eagle appeared following Hercules’s prayer. Chosen by lot to fight Hector, he fought until heralds stopped the combat at night, defended the Greek ships, rescued Patroclus’ body, and carried Achilles’ body while Odysseus fought attackers. He then lost Achilles’ arms to Odysseus, went mad, killed cattle and herdsmen, and killed himself; Agamemnon forbade his burning, and he was buried in a coffin at Rhoeteum. Another account links his impiety against Athena to his death at sea after Poseidon split the rock on which he survived a thunderbolt; Thetis buried him at Myconos.

is_a son [of Telamon and Hesione] Teucer, son of the river Scamander and the nymph Idaea, ruled the country to which Dardanus came. He welcomed Dardanus, gave him part of the land and Batia as a wife, and after Teucer died Dardanus called the whole country Dardania.

Telamon is a son, described as born either to Aeacus and Endeis or to Actaeus and Glauce. After killing Phocus with a quoit, he was exiled from Aegina. He succeeded Cychreus as king of Salamis, married Periboea and fathered Ajax, received Hesione from the expedition against Troy, and fathered Teucer with her.

Patroclus is a person, chiefly described as Menoetius’s son, Achilles’s companion and beloved, a Myrmidon, and a suitor of Helen; another record lists him as Hercules’s son by Pyrippe. After killing Cleitonymus in a knucklebones quarrel, he flees with his father to Peleus. At Troy, sent in Achilles’ armor to defend burning ships, he kills Sarpedon and others, is wounded by Euphorbus, killed by Hector, and honored with funeral games.

Tyndareus’s oath bound Helen’s suitors to defend the bridegroom chosen for her against anyone who wronged him over the marriage. Odysseus proposed it to prevent quarrels, Tyndareus imposed it, and later Agamemnon invoked the kings’ oaths after Helen’s abduction.
Tyndareus chose Menelaus as Helen’s bridegroom after obtaining the oath of her suitors. The kings of Greece had gathered at Sparta to seek Helen’s hand.
Messene is a place from which Castor and Pollux carried off and married Leucippus’s daughters, then attacked to recover booty.
The sons of Aphareus were Idas and Lynceus. They joined Castor and Pollux in driving cattle booty from Arcadia, and later opposed the Dioscuri in the conflict over the spoil.
Cattle booty was driven from Arcadia by Castor, Pollux, Idas, and Lynceus; Idas divided it, consumed his and his brother’s shares, drove it to Messene, and Dioscuri recovered it with other spoil.

Heaven is the sky, an upper world and source of fire. It matters most as a remote place people, animals, birds, insects, and Prometheus reach or enter to obtain fire. Earth people make arrows into a ladder or chain, or tear a hole in it; a spider’s thread reaches it, and the woodpecker and man descend after gaining fire.
Immortality is the boon Demeter tries to bestow on the infant by placing him on the fire. Her purpose is frustrated when a mortal interrupts the rite.

l: alternation of divine and mortal existence, The Library
s: After Castor’s death, Pollux refused to accept immortality without his brother. Zeus therefore granted Castor and Pollux existence on alternating days among the gods and mortals.
Stars are transformed animals killed in the war and Earth people left in the sky after the chain breaks, becoming visible there.
Iasion, son of Electra and Zeus, loved Demeter but was killed by a thunderbolt while attempting to defile her.

Dardanus, son of Electra and Zeus and brother of Iasion, left Samothrace grieving Iasion, reached the mainland, married Batia, received land from Teucer, founded Dardanus, and named the country Dardania.

Demeter arrives in Attica during Pandion’s reign and is welcomed by Celeus at Eleusis. In the fire rite story, Celeus and Metanira are her parents. She tries to make infant Demophon or Triptolemus immortal by fire, but is interrupted; accounts differ on the child’s fate. She gives wheat to Triptolemus, who reveals corn to mankind.
Dardanus left Samothrace after the death of his brother Iasion and went to the opposite mainland.
was_named_after Dardanus [the whole country, after Teucer’s death] Dardania was the name Dardanus gave to the whole country after Teucer died.

Ilus, son of Dardanus and king of Ilium, went to Phrygia, won a wrestling contest and fifty youths and maidens, followed a dappled cow, founded Ilium where it lay down, and received the Palladium after praying to Zeus.

Erichthonius is described in differing accounts as son of Dardanus, succeeding the childless Ilus and fathering Tros by Astyoche; or as son of Hephaestus with Atthis or Athena. Raised by Athena and intended for immortality, he expels Amphictyon, becomes king of Athens, establishes Athena’s wooden image and the Panathenaea, marries Praxithea, fathers Pandion, and is buried in Athena’s precinct.
Tros, son of Erichthonius and Astyoche, succeeded to the kingdom, named the country Troy, and with Callirrhoe fathered Cleopatra, Ilus, Assaracus, and Ganymede.

Troy is a city named after Tros, with Priam’s palace among its places. Its central story is the Trojan war: after Alexander carries Helen away from Sparta, the Greeks assemble an expedition. They first mistake Mysia for Troy, then, after Telephus shows them the route, sail toward Troy when the Trojans refuse to restore Helen and the property. The Greeks shut the Trojans inside the city and besiege it. Calchas says that capture will take ten years and cannot occur without Achilles; Achilles comes to Troy after Odysseus finds him at Lycomedes’s court. During the war, Alexander is wounded by Philoctetes with Heracles’ bows and dies while being carried back to Troy. After nine years, allies defend Troy, drive the Greeks behind their wall, breach it, and burn the ships. Memnon arrives with Ethiopians, and Troy becomes the setting for battles among Memnon, Achilles, Ajax, and the other forces. Yet the city cannot be taken while the Palladium remains inside it; capture also requires the bones of Pelops, Neoptolemus’s aid, and the bow of Hercules. In the end, the Greeks use the Wooden Horse, stationed beside Priam’s palace. They emerge from it, open the gates, kill the inhabitants, burn Troy, carry away and divide its spoils, and lay it waste before sailing away. Afterward, Troy remains a destination for the Locrian maidens sent to propitiate Athena, who are pursued by its inhabitants and take refuge in the sanctuary; it is also the place of the siege from which Idomeneus returns.
is_parent_of Capys [with Hieromneme] Assaracus was a son of Tros and Callirrhoe. With Hieromneme, daughter of Simoeis, he fathered Capys.
Ganymede, son of Tros and Callirrhoe, is carried away by Zeus on an eagle because of his beauty and becomes cupbearer of the gods in heaven.
is_parent_of Anchises [with Themiste] Capys was the son of Assaracus and Hieromneme. With Themiste, daughter of Ilus, he fathered Anchises.
Anchises, son of Capys and Themiste, joins Aphrodite in love and fathers Aeneas and Lyrus.

Aphrodite is a goddess whose actions center on desire, beauty, and aid to favored people. Angered by Smyrna’s failure to honor her, she causes Smyrna’s passion for her father, conceals the infant Adonis, and later receives part of his year. She loves Anchises and bears Aeneas and Lyrus, wins Alexander’s choice by offering Helen, rescues him from Menelaus, and is wounded while helping Aeneas.
Aeneas, son of Anchises and Aphrodite, possesses cattle, flees Troy carrying Anchises, and is spared by Greeks because of his piety.
Ilus went to Phrygia and won a wrestling contest held by the king there. He then followed the dappled cow to the hill of the Phrygian Ate, where he founded Ilium.

lay_down_at hill of the Phrygian Ate The king gave Ilus a dappled cow and instructed him to found a city wherever it lay down. The cow lay down at the hill of the Phrygian Ate, and Ilus founded Ilium there.

Ilium is a place founded by Ilus where a dappled cow lay down. After Ilus prayed to Zeus, the Palladium appeared; Zeus had thrown it into the land, and Ilus built it a temple. The image’s presence protected Ilium: it could not be taken until it was stolen. Helenus said its capture also required the bones of Pelops for the Greeks and Neoptolemus to fight. Athena was to be propitiated there. Heracles and Telamon captured the city earlier; later the Greeks sacked and destroyed it after the Trojan War. Odysseus begins his wanderings from Ilium.

The Palladium is a three-cubit wooden image made by Athena in the likeness of Pallas, with an aegis around its breast, joined feet, an upright spear in its right hand, and a distaff and spindle in the other. Connected with Pallas, daughter of Triton, it was granted by Zeus to Ilus: it fell from heaven, appeared before Ilus’s tent after his prayer, and came into Ilium, where Ilus built it a temple and honored it. It protected Troy so long as it remained within the walls. During the ten-year war, Helenus said Troy could not be taken until it was stolen; Odysseus, Diomedes, and Ulysses are said to have taken it to the ships.
Pallas, Triton’s daughter raised by him, trained in war with Athena and fathered fifty sons; startled by Zeus’s aegis while attacking Athena, she was wounded by Athena.
Memnon, son of Tithonus and Eos, leads Ethiopians to Troy, kills many Achaeans including Antilochus, and is killed by Achilles.
Podarces, Laomedon’s son, becomes king of Ilium after Heracles captures it and is called Priam.

Priam, formerly called Podarces, is the son of Laomedon and becomes king of Ilium after Heracles captures it; Heracles spares him and Hesione redeems him. He first marries Arisbe, with whom he has Aesacus, then marries Hecuba, who bears Hector, Polites, Paris, and other children. He also has many sons and daughters by other women. After learning Hecuba’s dream, he summons Aesacus and follows advice to expose a newborn child. As Hector’s father and Hecuba’s husband, he later ransoms Hector’s body after Hector’s death. During the Greek attack and sack of Troy, Priam seeks refuge at the altar of Zeus of the Courtyard, where Neoptolemus kills him.
Aesacus, son of Priam and Arisbe, learned dream interpretation from Merops; summoned to interpret Hecuba’s dream, he warned that her child would ruin the country and advised exposing the infant.

Hecuba is described as Dymas’s daughter and Priam’s second wife. She bears many children, including Hector, Paris, Creusa, Laodice, Polyxena, Cassandra, Deiphobus, Helenus, Pammon, Polites, Antiphus, Hipponous, Polydorus, and Troilus, who is said to have been fathered by Apollo. Before another birth, she dreams of a fiery firebrand burning the whole city. After Troy, she is awarded to Ulysses, though another account gives her to Helenus, who takes her to the Chersonese. There she becomes a bitch and is buried at Bitch’s Tomb; she is also called an attendant of Hecate.

Hector, firstborn son of Priam and Hecuba and husband of Andromache, is a warrior who kills Protesilaus, challenges Ajax and fights him, breaches the Greek wall and ditch, and sets fire to ships. After killing Patroclus, he is slain by Achilles; Priam later ransoms his body.

Paris, son of Priam and Hecuba, was born after Hecuba’s dream of a firebrand. Ordered exposed on Ida, he was nursed by a bear, found and raised by Agelaus, and surnamed Alexander for defending flocks. He later carried a phantom of Helen to Troy in ships built by Phereclus.

Alexander is the later name of Paris, a young man marked by beauty and strength after he defended flocks and repelled robbers. He marries Oenone, then judges the contest among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite, choosing Aphrodite after her promise of Helen. He sails to Sparta, persuades or abducts Helen, and brings her, or, in an alternative account, a cloud-made phantom, to Troy after time in Phoenicia and Cyprus. During the war he fights Menelaus in single combat but is carried away by Aphrodite when losing. Philoctetes wounds him with the bow of Hercules. Alexander returns to Oenone seeking treatment, but she refuses; he is carried toward Troy and dies, later described as shot and killed by the healed Philoctetes.

l: Hecuba's dream of the firebrand, The Library
s: Hecuba dreams she gives birth to a fiery firebrand that spreads and burns the entire city; Aesacus interprets the dream as foretelling a child’s ruin of the country.
Paris, son of Priam and Hecuba, is judged a danger because of Hecuba’s dream and ordered exposed on Ida. A bear nurses him for five days; Agelaus finds him alive and raises him as his child.
Daughter of Priam and Hecuba, Polyxena is slaughtered by Greeks on the grave of Achilles.

Cassandra, daughter of Priam and Hecuba, becomes a prophetess when Apollo teaches her prophecy in exchange for favours. After she refuses him, he leaves her prophecies unable to persuade others. She correctly warns the Trojans that the Wooden Horse contains armed forces, but they ignore her. Ajax the Locrian violates her at Athena’s image, and Agamemnon later receives her as an award.
Cassandra learns prophecy from Apollo, but Apollo deprives it of the power to persuade after she refuses his favours.
Deiphobus quarrelled with Helenus over marriage to Helen and was preferred over him.

Helenus is a seer who knew oracles protecting Troy. After Deiphobus was preferred over him in marriage to Helen, he left Troy for Ida, was captured by Odysseus, and under compulsion revealed how Ilium could be taken. In one account he received Hecuba, crossed to Chersonese, and buried her. He later traveled with Neoptolemus to Molossia, married Deidamia, and founded and inhabited a city there.
is_killed_by Achilles [in the sanctuary of Thymbraean Apollo] Achilles waylaid Troilus in the sanctuary of Thymbraean Apollo and killed him.
Bias, Talaus's son, sought marriage to Pero, persuaded Melampus to obtain Phylacus's kine, and married Pero after Melampus brought them to Neleus.

Idomeneus is a king of Crete who rules there and leads his army at the siege of Troy. Returning from Troy, he vows to Neptune to sacrifice whoever first meets him. Accounts differ on whether he sacrifices or only attempts to sacrifice his son, and on his expulsion: he is banished after a pestilence or expelled by Leucus. Exiled from Crete, he settles in Sallentine land. His legends are cited as possible evidence of sacrificial-vow custom.
Daughter of Eetion, Andromache marries Hector, is awarded to Neoptolemus after Troy’s sack, and bears him Molossus.

Oenone, daughter of Cebren, learns prophecy from Rhea and can heal wounded people with drugs. She warns Alexander not to sail for Helen and says only she can heal him. When he returns wounded, resentment makes her refuse treatment; she later brings medicines, finds him dead, and hangs herself.
᾿Αναχθέντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἀπ᾽ Ἄργους καὶ παραγε-] The bow of Heracles was in Philoctetes’ possession when Odysseus abandoned him on Lemnos. Philoctetes used it there to shoot birds for food.

Asopus is a river god whose parentage is given variously as Ocean and Tethys, Poseidon and Pero, or Zeus and Eurynome. He marries Metope and fathers Ismenus, Pelagon or Pelasgus, and twenty daughters, including Aegina. After Zeus carries Aegina away, Asopus pursues him to Corinth, but Zeus drives him back to his own streams with thunderbolts.
Aegina, daughter of Asopus and Metope, is one of their twenty daughters; Zeus abducts her to Oenone and fathers Aeacus with her.

l: Alexander’s voyage to Helen, The Library
s: Oenone warns Alexander not to sail for Helen. He does not heed her and abducts Helen from Sparta.

The Trojan War is a ten-year Greek expedition and siege against Troy, involving Trojans and a mustered Greek army. Telephus shows the Greeks the way, and Philoctetes brings Heracles’ bow. Fighting includes Achilles’ campaigns around Troy, arriving Trojan allies, Alexander’s combat with Menelaus, battles involving Diomedes, Ajax, Hector, Patroclus, and Achilles, and the burning of Greek ships. Alexander is wounded and dies after Oenone initially refuses treatment; Priam ransoms and buries Hector. As Greeks despair in the tenth year, the Wooden Horse leads to Troy’s fall.
Pero, exceptionally beautiful daughter of Neleus, is promised for recovering kine and becomes Bias’s bride after Melampus brings them to Pylus.
Formerly called Oenone, it was named Aegina; Zeus and Aegina had Aeacus there, and Zeus made its ants into men for him.

Aeacus, son of Zeus and Aegina, married Endeis and fathered Peleus, Telamon, and Phocus. Most pious of men, he prayed for Greece during infertility. After Phocus's murder, he drove Peleus and Telamon from Aegina; after death, he was honored in Pluto's abode and guarded Hades's keys.

Sciron is a Corinthian man, said to be son of Pelops or, in some accounts, Poseidon. At the Scironian Rocks in the Megarian region, he forces passersby to wash his feet, then throws them into the sea for his enormous turtle. Theseus ultimately seizes Sciron by the feet and throws him into the sea.

Peleus is a mortal hero, son of Aeacus and Endeis and brother of Telamon. With Telamon he plotted against Phocus and concealed him in a wood, leading to exile from Aegina. In Phthia, Eurytion purified him, gave him Antigone and a third of his country, but Peleus accidentally killed Eurytion during the Calydonian boar hunt and fled to Iolcus, where Acastus purified him. After Astydamia’s false accusation, Acastus abandoned him on Pelion and hid his sword; Chiron saved Peleus and restored it. Peleus joined the Argonauts, wrestled with Atalanta, later married Polydora and then Thetis, and received Chiron’s ash spear and the immortal horses Balius and Xanthus from Poseidon. He fathered Achilles with Thetis and brought the infant to Chiron after Thetis left; he also brought the blinded Phoenix to Chiron, who healed him, and made Phoenix king of the Dolopians. Peleus gave refuge to Patroclus, joined Jason and the Dioscuri in sacking Iolcus, and killed Astydamia. Expelled from Phthia by Acastus’s sons, he died and was buried in Icos; Neoptolemus then succeeded to his father’s kingdom.

is_author_of Melampus and the kine of Phylacus [the seventh book] Pherecydes was cited as the authority for the story in the seventh book of his work. The account attributed to him includes Melampus's imprisonment, the worms' warning, the consultation of the birds, and Iphiclus's cure.
Cychreus, son of Poseidon and Salamis, became king of Salamis by killing its ravaging snake, then died childless and gave the kingdom to Telamon.
Phocus, son of Aeacus and Psamathe, excels in athletic contests; Peleus and Telamon plot against him, and Telamon kills him with a quoit.

suffered_from infertility of Greece [because of Pelops's crime against Stymphalus] Greece suffered infertility because Pelops had killed Stymphalus, king of the Arcadians, and scattered his limbs. Oracles declared that Greece would be freed from its troubles if Aeacus prayed on its behalf, and the infertility ended after he did so.

Pelops, son of Tantalus, was slaughtered and boiled at a banquet of the gods, then restored to life fairer than before. His beauty made him Poseidon’s beloved and minion, and Poseidon gave him a winged chariot. He married Hippodamia, fathered Atreus and Thyestes, succeeded to Mycenae, subjugated Apia and Pelasgiotis, and named Peloponnesus after himself. He killed Stymphalus while feigning friendship, scattering his limbs and causing Greece’s infertility. Later, his bones were required before Ilium could be taken.

Hades is an abode ruled by Pluto. Theseus and Pirithous descend there; Hades deceives them into sitting on the Chair of Forgetfulness, which holds them fast. Hercules finds Pirithous but cannot rescue him, and Theseus remains detained. It contains punishments and the stone of Ascalaphus; people are returned from it, while dead souls flee Hercules and are seen by Ulysses.
The murder of Phocus was committed by Telamon, with Peleus helping to carry and hide the body. After the murder was discovered, Aeacus drove Peleus and Telamon from Aegina.
Salamis, Asopus's daughter and snake-ravaged island, is ruled by Cychreus, who kills it; childless, he yields to Telamon.
Acastus, king of Iolcus and husband of Astydamia, purified Peleus, then after Astydamia accused Peleus, abandoned him hunting on Pelion and hid his sword; he is also reported parent of Sthenelus.

sends Jason [to fetch the Golden Fleece] Pelias sends Jason to fetch the Golden Fleece. When Jason returns to Iolcus, he receives the Golden Fleece from him; Medea later beguiles Pelias’s daughters into murdering their father.
Astydamia, Acastus’s wife, falls in love with Peleus and proposes a meeting; after his refusal, she falsely accuses him to Acastus. Peleus later kills her and has her body cut apart.

hosted hunt on Pelion [hunting ground] Pelion was the place where Acastus took Peleus for a hunt and later abandoned him asleep. Peleus was threatened by centaurs there, but Chiron rescued him and found and returned his sword.
Centaurs, Hippodamia’s kinsmen, attend Pirithous’s wedding, become drunk and attack her; battle with Pirithous and Theseus kills many.

Thetis is a Nereid, sea-goddess, and daughter of Nereus. Zeus and Poseidon sought her in marriage until a prophecy said her son would be mightier than his father. Peleus pursued her; she changed into fire, water, and beasts to escape, but he held her until she returned to her original form, and they married on Mount Pelion. She became Peleus’s sea-bride and the mother of Achilles. She tried secretly to make Achilles immortal, placing him in fire at night and anointing him with ambrosia by day, but Peleus interrupted or reproached her; she left him and returned to the Nereids. Foreseeing Achilles’s death if he went to war, she disguised him as a girl and placed him with Lycomedes, and later warned him not to kill Tenes or be first to land at Troy. She is also said to save Hephaestus, help guide the Argo through the Wandering Rocks, and advise and protect Achilles and Neoptolemus. In one tradition she is Neoptolemus’s mother and tells him to remain in Tenedos two days before traveling to Molossia.
Prometheus takes fire and mechanical arts from Athena and Hephaestus’s workshop, gives them to men, and is nailed to Caucasus.

Hera is a daughter of Cronus and Rhea, wife of Zeus, and mother of Hephaestus. Cronus swallowed her; Zeus later put her in bonds and hung her from Olympus, though he feared her. She receives golden apples on her marriage with Zeus and competes with Athena and Aphrodite for the prize of beauty, offering Alexander dominion over all men; afterward she sends a severe storm against Alexander and Helen. Repeatedly desired, wooed, assaulted, or attacked by Ixion, Ephialtes, and Porphyrion, she reports Ixion to Zeus, who creates a cloud in her likeness. Hera’s actions chiefly harm or oppose others: she persecutes Io, delays Alemena’s delivery, sends serpents against infant Hercules, drives Hercules, Athamas, and Ino mad, deceives Semele, sends the Sphinx to Thebes, and blinds Tiresias after he arbitrates her dispute with Zeus. Yet she helps the Argonauts and is eventually reconciled with Hercules.

l: The Marriage of Peleus and Thetis, The Library
s: The Marriage of Peleus and Thetis is a Greek myth marriage story, known through Apollodorus and listed as the tenth appendix heading. It takes place on Pelion, where the gods celebrate with feast and song; Chiron gives Peleus an ashen spear and Poseidon immortal horses. A comparison with a modern Cretan tale suggests that Thetis later vanishes into the sea after Peleus reproaches her while she tries to make their child immortal.
The Pelian spear is the weapon with which Achilles wounds Telephus. Achilles scrapes it to obtain the rust used to heal Telephus's wound.

Achilles is a hero and Greek warrior, son of Peleus and Thetis, earlier named Ligyron and raised by Chiron on the inwards of lions and wild swine and the marrow of bears. At nine, he was declared necessary for Troy’s capture. To conceal him, Thetis disguised him as a maiden and entrusted him to Lycomedes; there he had a child with Deidamia. Once discovered, he traveled to Troy with Phoenix and Patroclus, becoming admiral and leader of the Myrmidons’ fifty ships. He was linked to Iphigenia as her supposed bridegroom, killed Tenes despite Thetis’s warning, and, after Protesilaus died, landed with the Myrmidons. He killed Cycnus and Troilus, captured Lycaon, seized cities including Lesbos and Lyrnessus, and fought around Troy for years. Anger over Briseis led him to refuse battle until Patroclus fought and was killed. Achilles then received armor from Hephaestus, returned to war, killed many Trojans including Hector, Penthesilia, and Memnon, and dragged Hector’s body to the ships. He was killed at the Scaean gate when Alexander and Apollo shot him in the ankle. Buried with Patroclus in the White Isle, with their bones mixed, he was later said to consort with Medea in the Isles of the Blest. His grave became the place of Polyxena’s sacrifice, and his arms were awarded to Ulysses after his death.
Nereids are sea nymphs who inhabit a cave, carry a young man there for his music, and reject a sea-maiden after motherhood.

Jason, son of Aeson, dwells in Iolcus and is sent by Pelias to fetch the Golden Fleece. As admiral of the Argo, he sails with Zetes and Calais, beds with Hypsipyle, demands the fleece from Aeetes, yokes brazen-footed bulls, sows dragon’s teeth, and wins it with Medea’s help. He swears to marry Medea, flees and marries her in Corcyra, returns the fleece to Pelias, is expelled from Iolcus, then goes to Corinth, marries Glauce, divorces Medea, and helps Peleus lay waste to Iolcus.

Calchas is a diviner who interprets signs and prophecies concerning the Greeks’ war against Troy. At Aulis he reads the serpent and sparrows as Zeus’s sign that Troy will fall after ten years, but says the Greeks cannot sail unless Iphigenia is sacrificed to Artemis. During the war he declares that Achilles and Hercules’ bow and arrows are required to capture Troy, and that Helenus knows the city’s protective oracles. After Troy is destroyed, he delays the Greeks because Athena is angry at Ajax’s impiety. He travels to Colophon, loses a divination contest to Mopsus, dies, and is buried at Notium.
has_daughter Deidamia Lycomedes received Achilles from Thetis and kept him at his court disguised as a maiden. His daughter Deidamia had a son by Achilles there.
is_daughter_of Lycomedes Deidamia, daughter of Lycomedes, had a son named Pyrrhus by Achilles while he was being brought up at her father’s court.

Neoptolemus, also called Pyrrhus, is Achilles’ son and later a king of the Molossians. Sought at Scyros by Odysseus and Phoenix, he is brought to fight for the Greeks, kills many Trojans and Eurypylus, and receives Andromache as a special award; tradition also places Polyxena’s death at his hands on Achilles’ grave. After waiting at Tenedos to sacrifice, he journeys toward Molossia, buries Phoenix, defeats and rules the Molossians, and fathers Molossus by Andromache. He succeeds Peleus, marries Hermione after carrying her off, gives Deidamia to Helenus, and is killed by Machaereus in an alternative tradition after attacking a sanctuary.
Calchas declared that Troy could not be captured without Achilles. Thetis foresaw that Achilles would die if he went campaigning.

Phoenix, son of Amyntor, was blinded after a concubine’s false accusation, restored by Chiron, made king of the Dolopians by Peleus, fathered Adonis according to Hesiod, and accompanied Achilles to Troy.

Cecrops, autochthonous and compounded of man and serpent, is Attica’s first king, renaming it Cecropia. He testifies for Athena’s claim to Attica and her planting of the olive-tree. He marries Agraulus, has Erysichthon and daughters Agraulus, Herse, and Pandrosus, and is father of Pandion. After his death, Cranaus becomes king.

Attica, formerly Acte and renamed Cecropia by its first king Cecrops, was awarded to Athena over Poseidon, who flooded it; Cranaus succeeded Cecrops, and under Pandion Dionysus taught Icarius wine-making after coming with Demeter.

contains Erechtheis [a sea produced by Poseidon] The sisters of Pandrosus opened the chest containing Erichthonius and, after seeing the infant with a serpent, were either destroyed by the serpent or driven mad and threw themselves down from the acropolis. Erichthonius later set up the wooden image of Athena on the acropolis.

is_shown_in the Pandrosium [still shown there] The olive-tree was planted by Athena in Attica and was shown in the Pandrosium. Its planting served as evidence in the contest between Athena and Poseidon.

l: the contest for Attica, The Library
s: The contest for Attica was between Poseidon and Athena; Zeus appointed twelve gods, who awarded it to Athena after Cecrops testified she first planted the olive-tree.

Athens is a city named by Athena after the twelve gods awarded her Attica. After Cecrops, Cranaus came to the throne; Erichthonius became king, established the Panathenaea, and set Athena’s wooden image on the acropolis. It was defended by Erechtheus, then ruled by Aegeus after the sons of Pandion expelled the Metionids. Minos attacked it, and its people were required to send youths and maidens to the Minotaur. Theseus arrived there, took control of its government, and led the Athenians against the Amazons. Later the Dioscuri captured Athens, gave sovereignty to Menestheus, and Theseus was driven out. It also contains Ogre and was where another modern Greek story was recorded.
Pandrosus, daughter of Cecrops, is entrusted by Athena with a forbidden chest containing Erichthonius; unlike her curious sisters, she is not said to open it.
Cephalus, Deion's son, is carried by Dawn to Syria, marries Procris, reconciles after her affair, accidentally kills her hunting with a dart, and is perpetually banished.

Phaethon, son of Clymene and the Sun and father of Astynous, asks to drive the Sun’s chariot for a day. A helpless, imprudent charioteer, he loses control, burns the earth, and is struck by Jove’s thunderbolt, falling into Eridanus.

Cinyras, son of Sandocus and Pharnace, comes to Cyprus with his people, founds Paphos, and marries Metharme. They have Oxyporus, Adonis, Orsedice, Laogore, and Braesia. He gives breastplates to absent Agamemnon, promises fifty ships to the Greek expedition, but sends one under a son of Mygdalion and molds the rest from earth before launching them at sea.
Agapenor, Phidippus with the Coans, and Demophon with his followers settled in Cyprus. Demophon went there after leaving Phyllis, and his followers settled there after his death.

Adonis is a boy and infant in accounts of disputed parentage: Hesiod names Phoenix and Alphesiboea, while another account names Cinyras and Metharme. He is born from the myrrh tree ten months after Smyrna's transformation, then concealed by Aphrodite. Zeus divides his year among himself, Persephone, and Aphrodite; Adonis gives his own share to Aphrodite. While still a boy, he is hunted, wounded, and killed by a boar during a hunt.
kills Adonis [by striking him while he is hunting] A boar strikes Adonis while he is hunting.
Assyrian king and Smyrna’s father, Thias unknowingly shares her bed for twelve nights, then discovers it and pursues her with a sword.
Smyrna, Thias’s daughter, is driven by Aphrodite’s wrath to desire and unknowingly sleep with her father for twelve nights; when pursued by him, she is transformed by the gods into a myrrh tree.
is_a tree [called smyrna] The myrrh tree is the form into which Smyrna is transformed. Ten months later, it splits open and Adonis is born from it.

Persephone is a woman associated with the underworld. Pluto carries her off and gives her a pomegranate seed before she is sent up. She keeps Adonis after receiving him from Aphrodite, though Zeus divides his year. Pirithous seeks to marry her, descending with Theseus and being detained in Hades.

l: Aphrodite and Persephone's dispute over Adonis, The Library
s: is_adjudicated_by Zeus Aphrodite entrusts the infant Adonis to Persephone, but Persephone refuses to return him after seeing him. The dispute is brought before Zeus for judgment.

l: Adonis's division of the year, The Library
s: divides the year [into three parts] Zeus divides the year into three parts for Adonis: one part by himself, one part with Persephone, and one part with Aphrodite.

l: Smyrna's passion for her father, The Library
s: Smyrna conceives a passion for her father as a result of Aphrodite's anger because Smyrna does not honour the goddess.

l: Smyrna's twelve-night intercourse with her father, The Library
s: With the help of her nurse, Smyrna shares her father's bed for twelve nights without his knowledge.

l: Smyrna's transformation into a tree, The Library
s: When Smyrna is pursued by her father after he discovers the intercourse, she prays to the gods to become invisible. The gods pity her and transform her into a myrrh tree.

l: Adonis's birth from the tree, The Library
s: Ten months after Smyrna becomes the myrrh tree, the tree splits open and Adonis is born from it.

l: Aphrodite's concealment of the infant Adonis, The Library
s: Because of Adonis's beauty, Aphrodite hides him as an infant in a chest, unknown to the gods, and entrusts him to Persephone.
is_caused_by the boar [after Adonis is struck while hunting] Adonis dies after being struck by a boar while hunting.

Cranaus, an autochthonous son of the soil, became king at Athens after Cecrops. He married Pedias and had children including Cranaichme, Cranae, Menaechme, and Atthis. During his reign Deucalion's flood occurred. After Atthis died unmarried, he named the country Atthis; Amphictyon later expelled him.
Deucalion reigns at Lycorea, flees to Cranaus for safety, sacrifices to Zeus, then a flood occurs during Cranaus's reign.
Deucalion’s flood, caused by heavy rains, is said to occur during Cranaus’s reign.

is_a virgin [at death] Atthis is a daughter of Cranaus. She dies while still a virgin, and Cranaus names the country Atthis after her. In one account, she is the mother of Erichthonius with Hephaestus.

Amphictyon is a king who expels Cranaus and rules in his place for twelve years. Accounts differ on his origin, calling him either a son of Deucalion or autochthonous, a son of the soil. His reign ends when Erichthonius expels him.

Hephaestus is a deity, born to Hera without intercourse and also described as son of Zeus and Hera. Lame, he is hurled from heaven by Zeus and falls to Lemnos. He shares a workshop with Athena, desires her, and is named father of Erichthonius, Palaemon, and Periphetes. He helps at Athena’s birth, kills Mimas, nails Prometheus to Caucasus, and reproaches him for stealing fire. A maker and giver, he makes weapons, Harmonia’s necklace, Achilles’ armour, gives Talos to Minos, dries Scamander, and is abandoned by Aphrodite.
Corn, Demeter’s beneficent gift to mankind, is described as spending six months in the earth and six above ground; Triptolemus reveals it to mankind.

Pandion is a king associated with Athens and later Megara. One account makes him king after Erichthonius died; another says he succeeded Cecrops, as Cecrops’ son by Metiadusa. During his reign Demeter and Dionysus came to Attica. He married Zeuxippe and had Procne, Philomela, Erechtheus, and Butes. In war with Labdacus over boundaries, he sought Tereus’ help, won, and gave Procne to Tereus. After his death, Erechtheus received the kingdom and Butes the priesthoods. Another account says he was expelled by Metion’s sons, went to Megara, married Pylia, became king there, and had Aegeus, Pallas, Nisus, and Lycus.

Dionysus is the offspring of Zeus and Semele, a deity whose life joins unusual birth, the vine and wine, travels and rites, and the elevation of Semele. Zeus carries him in his thigh after he is sewn there, entrusts him to Hermes, changes him into a kid, and he is reared as a girl by Athamas and Ino before being brought to the nymphs at Nysa. Dionysus discovers the vine, gives its plant to Oeneus, and gives Icarius a vine branch and teaches him wine-brewing when he comes to Attica during Pandion’s reign. Hera drives him mad; Rhea purifies him in Phrygia and teaches him initiation rites. He travels through Egypt, Syria, Thrace, India, Thebes, Argos, and elsewhere, spreads his rites, proves to the Thebans that he is a god, and is recognized as one. He is expelled by Lycurgus, drives Lycurgus mad, and turns pirates into dolphins. He loves Ariadne, carries her from Naxos to Lemnos, and fathers Thoas, Staphylus, Oenopion, and Peparethus with her. Finally, he resurrects Semele, names her Thyone, brings her up from Hades, and ascends with her to heaven.
Icarius’s daughter searches for his body, Maera guides her, and she mourns him before hanging herself.

results_from Hephaestus’s seed falling on the ground [after Athena wiped it from her leg with wool] When Athena fled from Hephaestus, his seed fell on her leg, and she wiped it off with wool and threw it onto the ground. As Athena fled and the seed fell to the ground, Erichthonius was produced.
Athena placed Erichthonius in a chest and entrusted it to Pandrosus, forbidding the chest to be opened. Pandrosus’s sisters nevertheless opened it out of curiosity and saw the infant with a serpent.

guards Erichthonius [coiled about him in the chest] A serpent was seen coiled around the infant Erichthonius when the sisters of Pandrosus opened his chest. According to one account it destroyed them; according to another, Athena’s anger drove them mad and caused them to throw themselves from the acropolis.
Erichthonius instituted the festival of the Panathenaea after becoming king of Athens.

l: arrival of Demeter and Dionysus in Attica, The Library
s: occurs_during_reign_of Pandion Demeter and Dionysus came to Attica during the reign of Pandion. Demeter was welcomed by Celeus at Eleusis, while Dionysus was received by Icarius.

Demeter was welcomed by Celeus at Eleusis when she came to Attica. Eumolpus fled to Eleusis after being detected in a plot against Tegyrius and made friends with the Eleusinians there. Eleusis was consequently involved in the later war against the Athenians.
Dionysus gave Icarius a vine branch and taught him about wine-making. Icarius then gave the resulting drink to shepherds.

is_caused_by shepherds [they mistook undiluted wine for witchcraft] Shepherds tasted the drink given to them by Icarius and drank it copiously without water. Believing themselves bewitched, they killed Icarius, though by day they understood what had happened and buried him.
is_by hanging [after the discovery of her father’s body] After Maera led Erigone to the buried body of Icarius, Erigone mourned her father and hanged herself.

Tereus, Ares’s Thracian son, helped Pandion defeat Labdacus, married Procne, and fathered Itys. After violating and mutilating Philomela, he pursued her and Procne after Itys was served to him, ending transformed into a hoopoe.
Daughter of Pandion, Procne marries Tereus and bears Itys; after learning of Philomela's suffering, she kills and serves Itys to Tereus, then becomes a nightingale fleeing with Philomela.
Philomela, Pandion’s daughter and Procne’s sister, is violated and silenced by Tereus, reveals her suffering through woven letters, flees with Procne, and is transformed into a swallow.

Erechtheus, twin son of Pandion, became king after receiving the kingdom as his inheritance. He married Praxithea and had three sons and four daughters. In war with the Eleusinians, an oracle required the slaughter of one daughter for victory; he sacrificed his youngest daughter, after which the others killed themselves. He killed Eumolpus in battle, then Poseidon killed him and destroyed his household.

is_ruled_by Leucus [after Leucus seduced ten cities from their allegiance] Crete was ruled by Idomeneus until Leucus seduced ten of its cities from their allegiance, made himself lord of the island, and expelled Idomeneus.
Itys, son of Tereus and Procne, is killed, cooked, and served by Procne to Tereus without his knowledge.
Daulia, a place in Phocis, was inhabited by Thracians and is identified with the pursuit and transformation of Procne, Philomela, and Tereus.

is_a Daulian bird [according to Greek poets cited by Thucydides] The nightingale is the transformed form of Procne. It continued to utter the cry associated with the moment of transformation and was said to flee while plaintively calling the name of her dead son, Itys.
is_a bird [after transformation of Tereus] The hoopoe is the transformed form of Tereus. It continued to pursue his cruel wife after the transformation.
is_a bird [after transformation of Philomela] The swallow is the transformed form of Philomela.
In Daulia, Procne and Philomela prayed to the gods while Tereus pursued them; all became birds: nightingale, swallow, and hoopoe.
was_committed Itys [by Procne] After learning of Philomela's suffering, Procne killed Itys, cooked him, and served him to Tereus, who was unaware that the meal was his son's body.

involved tongue [Tereus cut it out] After violating Philomela and telling her that Procne was dead, Tereus cut out her tongue and concealed her. Philomela then conveyed her suffering to Procne by weaving letters into a garment.

Procris, a hunter and wife of Cephalus, used Circaean root against Minos after fleeing there following her affair with Pteleon. She reconciled with Cephalus, but he accidentally killed her with a dart while hunting.
Orithyia, daughter of Erechtheus, is carried off by Boreas while playing by the Ilissus and becomes mother of Cleopatra, Chione, Zetes, and Calais.
Boreas carries off Orithyia by the Ilissus and fathers Cleopatra, Chione, Zetes, and Calais, including winged sons.
Pasiphae bewitches Minos, falls in love with Poseidon's bull, and receives Daedalus's help through a wooden cow.

Circe is an enchantress, daughter of Sun and Perse and sister of Aeetes, who lives on the Aeaean isle and knows all enchantments. She transforms Odysseus’s companions into animals, restores them after he resists her magic, and sends him onward with advice for passing the Sirens and avoiding the Wandering Rocks. Mother of Telegonus and married to Telemachus, she later receives Odysseus’s body and Penelope from Telegonus and sends Telegonus and Penelope to the Islands of the Blest.

Eumolpus is a son of Poseidon and Chione, thrown into the sea by his mother, rescued by Poseidon, carried to Ethiopia, and raised by Benthesicyme. He is associated with Ismarus, fluteplaying, and cleansing and initiating Hercules at Eleusis. Banished, he goes to Tegyrius and Thrace, later flees to the Eleusinians, returns to Tegyrius, and becomes king of Thrace. He fights for the Eleusinians against the Athenians and is killed by Erechtheus.

Athenians consult an oracle about victory, fight with Erechtheus against Eumolpus and the Eleusinians, and are promised victory if he sacrifices a daughter. During Minos’s war, famine and pestilence lead them to sacrifice Hyacinth’s daughters and yearly send seven youths and seven damsels to the Minotaur.
are_at_war_with Athenians The Eleusinians called on Eumolpus, who came with a large Thracian force to fight on their side against the Athenians. They were opposed by Erechtheus and the Athenians.

l: war between the Athenians and the Eleusinians, The Library
s: War between Athenians and Eleusinians begins when Eleusinians summon Eumolpus and a Thracian force; Erechtheus kills Eumolpus, then Poseidon destroys Erechtheus and his household.

l: sacrifice of Erechtheus's youngest daughter, The Library
s: An oracle declared that the Athenians would win the war if Erechtheus sacrificed one of his daughters. Erechtheus sacrificed his youngest daughter, and his other daughters also killed themselves because they had agreed to die together.

l: battle between Erechtheus and Eumolpus, The Library
s: After the sacrifice of Erechtheus’s youngest daughter and the deaths of his other daughters, the battle took place. Erechtheus killed Eumolpus, but Poseidon then killed Erechtheus and destroyed his household.

requires_sacrifice_of daughters of Erechtheus [as the condition for Athenian victory] The oracle told Erechtheus that the Athenians would win if he sacrificed one of his daughters. It later told Aegeus to loosen the bulging mouth of the wineskin only after reaching the height of Athens, and told the Athenians to give Minos whatever satisfaction he chose.
Megara received Pandion after he was expelled from Athens. Pylas gave its kingdom to Pandion before departing for Peloponnese, and Minos later captured Megara while Nisus was king.

Aegeus, described chiefly as Pandion’s son, holds the whole power after a divided government, though some accounts call Scyrius his father. After marriages to Meta and Chalciope and having no child, he consults an oracle, goes to Troezen, and fathers Theseus with Aethra. He leaves a sword and sandals beneath a rock for the child, but later fails to recognize Theseus and sends him against the Marathonian bull. Theseus’s sword reveals him; Aegeus knocks away Medea’s poisoned cup and expels her. He orders white sails for Theseus’s safe return, sees black instead, believes him dead, and dies.
Nisus, Pandion’s son and king of Megara, bore a fated purple hair whose removal meant death; when his daughter Scylla pulled it out in treachery, he died.

Neoptolemus was killed at Delphi. In another account, he went to Delphi to demand satisfaction from Apollo for his father’s death, plundered the votive offerings, and burned the temple. Delphi was the site of the oracle that gave guidance on many mythological events. Orestes was tried there after killing Neoptolemus, and he later slew Neoptolemus at Delphi.
is_a city [on Aegeus’s route to Athens] Troezen was the place through which Aegeus passed on his return to Athens. There he lodged with Pittheus and encountered Aethra.
Pittheus, son of Pelops and king of Troezen, hosted Aegeus, understood an oracle, intoxicated him, and arranged his union with Aethra.
are_held_at Athens [as a festival] The Panathenian games were held in Athens, and Androgeus won against all competitors.

Androgeus, son of Minos, defeated all competitors at the Panathenian games. Aegeus sent him against the bull of Marathon, which killed him; another account says that jealous competitors ambushed and killed him while he was traveling to Thebes for the games in honor of Laius.
Poseidon’s bull kills Androgeus, is loved by Pasiphae, is sent against Theseus by Aegeus, and Theseus kills it.
Thebes, founded by Cadmus and named after Thebe, is ruled by Polydorus, Lycus, and Creon; afflicted by the Sphinx, it receives Oedipus, sees war, capture, abandonment, and Argive takeover.

Scylla is a sea monster dwelling in a cliff, daughter of Crataeis and of Trienus or Phorcus, with a woman’s face and breast, six dog heads, and twelve dog feet. She occupies one of two huge cliffs and, as Ulysses passes, seizes and eats six companions. Another account calls Scylla daughter of Nisus: loving Minos, she betrays her father and is drowned by Minos.

has black sail [before Theseus's return] The ship carries Theseus, Ariadne, and the rescued children from Crete toward Athens. Theseus forgets to change its black sail, leading Aegeus to believe that he has died.
afflicts Athens [during the war with Minos] Famine afflicted Athens during the prolonged war with Minos.
afflicts Athens [during the war with Minos] Pestilence afflicted Athens during the prolonged war with Minos.
Hyacinth's daughters Antheis, Aegleis, Lytaea, and Orthaea were sacrificial victims, slaughtered by Athenians on Geraestus's grave in accordance with an ancient oracle.

l: sacrifice of the daughters of Hyacinth, The Library
s: is_performed_by Athenians [in obedience to an ancient oracle] The Athenians performed the sacrifice of the daughters of Hyacinth to seek relief from the famine and pestilence afflicting Athens. The sacrifice was of no benefit, so they consulted the oracle again.

Minotaur is a bull-headed man, offspring of Pasiphae and a bull, confined by Minos in the Labyrinth. Each year it receives seven Athenian youths and seven maidens as food. In the third tribute Theseus is included; he finds Minotaur in the innermost Labyrinth and kills it.

l: seven Athenian youths and seven maidens, The Library
s: are_food_for Minotaur [sent without weapons] The Athenians were ordered by Minos to send seven youths and an equal number of maidens without weapons as food for the Minotaur.

The Labyrinth is a prison-like place of many winding turns, constructed by Daedalus to confine the Minotaur and prevent entrants from finding the way out. Each year, Athenians send seven youths and seven maidens there as food for the Minotaur. Daedalus reveals its exit route to Ariadne; Theseus enters with thread, kills the Minotaur, and follows the thread out. Later, Minos imprisons Daedalus and Icarus in the Labyrinth before pursuing Daedalus to Sicily.

Daedalus is an excellent architect, craftsman, and first inventor of images. He makes a statue of Heracles at Pisa and invents a saw by imitating a serpent’s jawbone. After killing Talos, his sister’s son, nephew, and pupil, by throwing him from the Acropolis, he is tried and condemned at the Areopagus and banished from Athens. He flees to Minos, assists Pasiphae by contriving a wooden cow, and constructs the Labyrinth, whose exit he knows. At Ariadne’s request, he reveals the way out and a thread plan. Minos then shuts Daedalus and his son Icarus in the Labyrinth. Daedalus makes wings for them, escapes, and flies to Camicus in Sicily, where Cocalus conceals him. Minos pursues and detects him after Daedalus devises a way to pass thread through a spiral shell. One record also says his corpse is discovered and he is tried at the Areopagus.
A road to Athens, guarded by criminal men and beset by evildoers until Theseus cleared it.

Periphetes, son of Hephaestus and Anticlia, was a weak-legged roadside evildoer called the Clubman or club-bearer for his iron club. He used it to kill passers-by until Theseus wrested it from him and killed him.
Epidaurus was the first place where Theseus killed an evildoer, Periphetes.
Periphetes used the iron club to kill passers-by; Theseus wrested it from him and continued carrying it.
Sinis, Polypemon and Sylea’s son, lives at the Isthmus of Corinth, forces passers-by to bend pine trees, and is killed by Theseus.
is_constructed_by Daedalus Daedalus contrives a wooden cow to assist Pasiphae after she falls in love with the bull of Poseidon.

l: the Isthmus of Corinth, The Library
s: The Isthmus of Corinth is an isthmus traversed by the Cretan bull, where Sinis forced passers-by to bend pine trees until Theseus killed him and cleared it of malefactors; the Argo is dedicated to Poseidon there, and it is linked to an oracle and chariot race.

toss_up passers-by [when the passers-by could not bend them] Sinis forced passers-by to keep bending pine trees. The passers-by were too weak to do so and were tossed up by the trees, perishing miserably.
Phaia, a sow raised by an old woman, was killed by Theseus at Crommyon; some accounts call Echidna and Typhon her parents.

l: Theseus's killing of Phaia, The Library
s: Theseus's killing of Phaia occurred at Crommyon, where he killed the sow called Phaia.

l: Theseus's killing of Sciron, The Library
s: Theseus killed Sciron by seizing him by the feet and throwing him into the sea.

Medea, described as Aeetes’ daughter and as his sister, is a witch who loves Jason. She gives Jason a magic drug, helps procure the Golden Fleece, flees and marries him, and murders her brother Apsyrtus. She beguiles Talos to death and causes Pelias’s daughters to murder Pelias. Divorced by Jason, she gives Glauce a poison-soaked robe, burns her, and murders her own children. Medea flees to Athens and marries Aegeus; while living with him, she plots against Theseus and provides poison for Aegeus, but is expelled after Theseus is recognized. She returns to Colchis, kills Perses, and restores Aeetes’ kingdom.
is_sent_to Minotaur [as the third tribute] The Cretan tribute includes Theseus as part of the third group sent to the Minotaur. Some say that Theseus volunteered for it.
The ship of Theseus has a black sail when it returns. Aegeus sees it from the acropolis and, believing Theseus has perished, kills himself.
Aegeus instructs Theseus to spread white sails if he returns alive. Theseus forgets to do so because he is grieving over Ariadne.
Ariadne, Minos’s daughter, loves Theseus and helps him seek the Labyrinth’s exit in exchange for marriage and passage to Athens. After leaving Crete with him, she is carried by Dionysus to Lemnos.

is_given_to Theseus [for entering and leaving the Labyrinth] Ariadne gives Theseus a clue of thread following Daedalus’s advice. Theseus fastens it to the door, unwinds it as he enters the Labyrinth, and uses it to find his way out after killing the Minotaur.
is_arrival_place_of Theseus [with Ariadne and the children] Theseus reaches Naxos at night with Ariadne and the children rescued from the Minotaur. Dionysus carries Ariadne away from there.
Lemnos is an island, called the source of fire in Cicero’s “Lemnian theft,” where Odysseus abandoned Philoctetes, who survived hunting birds, then returned with Diomedes for Heracles’ bow and arrows.
is_a sovereignty The Dioscuri gave the sovereignty of Athens to Menestheus after bringing him back.
Icarus, son of Daedalus and born to Naucrate, escaped the labyrinth with Daedalus using wings, ignored warning, flew too high, and died falling into Icarian Sea.

are_made_of glue [the glue melts in the sun] Daedalus constructed wings for himself and Icarus. He warned Icarus not to fly too high, lest the glue melt in the sun, or too near the sea, lest damp detach the pinions.
is_named_after Icarus The sea into which Icarus fell was called the Icarian Sea after him.
Cocalus, king at Camicus, shelters Daedalus, receives Minos while promising surrender, and lets his daughters kill Minos with boiling pitch.

Phaedra, daughter of Minos, marries Theseus and bears Acamas and Demophon. She becomes Hippolytus’s stepmother, loves him, seeks intercourse, falsely accuses him after rejection, and hangs herself when her passion becomes public.
is_in Sicily Camicus in Sicily was the place where Daedalus was concealed with Cocalus and where Minos came in pursuit of him.
Sicily is an island containing Trapani, where versions of the Ulysses and Polyphemus story may survive in oral tradition, including Sicilian and Albanian accounts.

l: flight of Theseus and his company, The Library
s: The flight of Theseus and his company caused Minos to imprison Daedalus and Icarus in the labyrinth.

l: Daedalus and Icarus’s flight, The Library
s: ends_in Icarus’s fall and death [after Icarus flies too high] Daedalus and Icarus escaped from the labyrinth by flying with wings made by Daedalus. Daedalus reached Camicus safely, but Icarus fell into the sea.

l: Icarus’s fall and death, The Library
s: occurs_in Icarian Sea Icarus's fall occurred after he disregarded Daedalus's injunction and flew too high. The glue melted in the sun, his wings fell apart, and he perished in the sea that was called the Icarian Sea.
